frase_gancho.texto: A place to look out over the Amatzinac valley and the outline of Popocatépetl.

guion_corto.texto: From here you look out over the valley. According to Grove, Popocatépetl can be seen from the site, and below stretches the valley of the Amatzinac River. If the day is clear, the volcano marks the horizon. Think about what you have walked through: a main terrace, a sunken patio, an altar-throne, a woman with outstretched arms and, on the slope, scenes of caves, rain and animals. The people who carved all of that lived between these hills and that valley, with water from a spring. For Grove, it was a cosmopolitan and autonomous regional center. Here the landscape explains the stones. Chalcatzingo means, among other possibilities, place of sacred water, according to INAH. Take a moment to breathe before going down.

guion_largo.texto:
You have reached the end of the tour. From this point you look out over the valley of the Amatzinac River and, when the day is clear, the outline of Popocatépetl.

First, the landscape. Chalcatzingo lies in eastern Morelos, at the foot of two hills. Below stretch the fields of the valley. A spring supplied the settlement, and a stream carries rainwater down the slope.

Now review what you saw, without hurry. The residential terraces, built around eight hundred years before Christ. The main plaza, the platform and the sunken patio. The altar-throne unlike any from the Gulf. The woman of Monument Twenty-One. The altar and stela pairs that point to southern Mesoamerica.

Then, the slope. A procession with feline masks. Supernatural beings that dominate people. A triad of felines found only a few years ago. And the cave where El Rey sits, surrounded by clouds and drops.

All of that was made in a very concentrated period. Almost all the monuments date from around seven hundred to five hundred years before Christ. They are the oldest stone sculptures known in the Central Highlands of Mexico.

Grove sums up his view in these words: neither Olmecs, nor mere imitators of La Venta. Chalcatzingo was a cosmopolitan and autonomous regional center that interacted with centers near and far. Possibly it did so to facilitate the circulation of greenstones and other exotic objects sought by emerging elites.

INAH recognizes another reading, that of Olmec influence. The debate remains open, and it is part of what makes this place interesting.

There is something this view makes clear. Water, hill and stone are not separate themes. They are the same subject: a people, at the foot of a hill with springs, who engraved in rock their ideas about the earth and the rain.

Arqueología Mexicana explains that, in the Morelos of those centuries, groups with a more complex social organization developed in places with abundant water. They also chose places where they could control springs and ravines. Looking at this valley, it is easy to understand why. From this spot you understand the whole site: the hill above, the terraces in the middle and the valley below.

If you take away three ideas, let them be these. First, that art changes according to place: political power on the terraces, myth and ritual on the hill. Second, that Chalcatzingo connected ideas from many regions. Third, that water and caves appear again and again.

In nineteen seventy-six and seventy-seven, Kenneth Hirth carried out surface surveys along the Amatzinac River. That kind of survey makes it possible to record settlements.

David Grove died in two thousand twenty-three, but the work continues. Since the year two thousand, INAH's Chalcatzingo Project, led by Mario Córdova with Carolina Meza, has been studying, conserving and presenting to the public the monument zone.

Thank you for walking through Chalcatzingo.

texto.pregunta: Myth: Everything at Chalcatzingo has been known for decades.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Monuments are still appearing, like the Triad of the Felines, found in two thousand eleven according to The History Blog.
